name: Custom software
description: A written scope, a fixed first increment, working software in your cloud inside six weeks. Then we keep going, or we hand it over with a runbook.
goodFor: A new product or module with a deadline
A rebuild the in-house team cannot fit in
An MVP that has to survive its first customers
gets: A two-page SOW three days after the call: what is in, what is out, what it costs
A fixed first increment: six weeks, working software in your cloud account
A fortnightly review you sign: shipped, slipped, cost against plan
A handover pack: runbook, tests, a recorded walkthrough, a week of questions answered
sayNoWhen: The deadline, the scope and the budget are all fixed and none of them can move
You want a team that builds whatever the spec says and never pushes back

steps.text: You describe the product. We say whether we are right for it and roughly what it costs.
Two pages: in, out, cost, acceptance criteria. Before you pay anything.
Repo, CI and environments in your cloud account; the first slice of the product under way.
Working software your users can touch, measured against the baseline.
Continue, change course or hand over. Your call, every fortnight.

faq.q: Who owns the code?
faq.a: You do, on payment of each invoice. It lives in your repo and your cloud account from day one, so there is nothing to transfer.

faq.q: What if the scope changes halfway through?
faq.a: It will. Changes go into the next increment, with the cost written down at the fortnightly review, so the first increment still lands on its date.

faq.q: Can you work with our in-house engineers?
faq.a: Yes, and we prefer it. They review our pull requests and we review theirs; the handover is shorter because nothing is new to them.

closing: Tell us what you want built. We will tell you what it costs.

name: Team augmentation
description: Named engineers in your standup from day one, on your repo and your board. We manage the person; you direct the work. Replacement inside ten working days if it is not working.

tiles.v: Years in production. No junior tier.

goodFor: Scaling a team without a six-month hiring round
A nine-month push with a hard date
Covering a leaver while you hire properly
gets: A named senior engineer, in your standup from day one, on your repo and your board
You meet the engineer before they start, and you can say no
We manage performance, holidays and cover; you direct the work
If it is not working, a replacement inside ten working days, and you do not pay for the overlap
sayNoWhen: You need a junior to clear the tickets nobody else wants
You want someone to be managed rather than someone who manages themselves

steps.text: What the team is building, what is slowing it down, and what good looks like in three months.
One or two named engineers, with the systems they have shipped. You interview them; you can say no.
Access, first commit, first review. Your tooling, your definition of done.
What landed, what slipped, what to change. A fifteen-minute call.
No argument, no buyout, no recruiter fee if you later hire them.

faq.q: How senior is senior?
faq.a: Years shipping to production, not years in the industry. Every engineer we place has owned a system in production and can show you which one.

faq.q: Which timezone do they work in?
faq.a: Four hours of overlap with GMT every working day, the same four hours, so your standup is never at midnight. US teams: we shift the day and agree the overlap in the SOW.

faq.q: Can we hire them permanently later?
faq.a: Yes. After six months there is no fee; before that, one month of the day rate. We would rather you had the person than a clause.

closing: Tell us who is missing. We will show you who we would send.

name: Data engineering & analytics
oneLiner: Pipelines and reporting people stop arguing with
description: Ingest, warehouse, models and dashboards that the in-house team can run after we leave. Measured before and after every increment.
goodFor: Reporting nobody trusts
A nightly batch that is now a daily problem
Numbers that differ by who ran the query
pageTitle:
Pipelines and reporting
people stop arguing with.
gets: Ingest and warehouse work the in-house team can run after we leave
One source of truth: a warehouse and a semantic layer, documented where your team looks
Dashboards the people who asked for them actually open
A before-and-after measurement on every increment
sayNoWhen: You want a dashboard before anyone agrees what the numbers mean
The data does not exist yet and nobody owns collecting it

steps.text: Sources, schedules, the queries people run by hand, and the two numbers that disagree.
How long the nightly run takes, how often it fails, and which report nobody trusts. Written down.
The worst pipeline replaced: incremental, idempotent, with a dead-letter queue and a replay.
Runbook, alerts and the on-call steps in your wiki; your team runs it for a week while we watch.
The same numbers as week one, after. Then the next pipeline, or the handover.

faq.q: Which warehouse?
faq.a: The one you have, unless it is the problem. We have shipped on PostgreSQL, Redshift, TimescaleDB and Athena over S3; we will say on the call if yours is the wrong tool.

faq.q: Do you do the dashboards too?
faq.a: Yes, and we start from the question the dashboard answers, not the chart. If nobody can say what decision it changes, we build the pipeline first and the dashboard last.

faq.q: What does measured mean here?
faq.a: A number from before, the same number from after, and the unit: run time, failure rate, freshness, the gap between two reports. It goes in the review you sign.

closing: Bring the report nobody trusts. We will tell you why.

name: AI & machine learning
oneLiner: Features that have to be right, not impressive
description: Retrieval, LLM features, classification and forecasting, each with an evaluation harness so you know when it got better and when it did not.
goodFor: An AI feature that has to be right, not impressive
Search or support that should answer from your data
Forecasts the finance team will actually use
pageTitle:
Features that have to be
right, not impressive.
gets: An evaluation harness before a demo: a number you can defend to your board
Retrieval done properly: chunking, ranking, citations, and the cases where it should say nothing
Cost and latency budgeted up front, then measured in production
Monitoring, retraining and rollout owned end to end, not handed to you as a notebook
sayNoWhen: The goal is an AI feature rather than a problem the feature solves
There is no data you are allowed to use, and no plan to get some

steps.text: What the model must get right, how often, and what happens when it is wrong.
A few hundred real cases, labelled with you. The number today, before any model.
Retrieval or classification in a staging environment, released only when the number moves.
Monitoring on quality, cost and latency; a retraining loop; a person in the loop where it matters.
The eval number, the bill and the latency, before and after. Then the next feature.

faq.q: Which models do you use?
faq.a: Whichever passes the eval at a cost you can afford. We have shipped on Claude, OpenAI, Gemini and Bedrock, and on small models where a large one was too expensive. The harness decides, not the logo.

faq.q: Will it hallucinate?
faq.a: Sometimes, which is why the harness exists. Retrieval with citations, refusal when the sources are thin, and a measured false-answer rate you can see every fortnight.

faq.q: Can you use our data without it leaving our account?
faq.a: Yes. Models run in your cloud account or through a provider with no training on your data, and the retrieval index lives with you.

closing: Tell us what it must get right. We will say how to measure it.

name: Cloud & DevOps
description: CI/CD, infrastructure as code, observability and cost control, set up so your team owns it afterwards and the on-call runbook is already written.
goodFor: Deploys that need a war room
A cloud bill nobody can explain
No runbook for the thing that pages you
gets: CI/CD with tests before features, not after the first incident
Infrastructure as code, reviewed like code, with a plan you can read before it applies
Observability you can act on, and a runbook for the thing that pages you
A cloud bill you can explain, line by line, and a smaller one
sayNoWhen: You want us to hold the pager forever instead of handing it back
Kubernetes is the goal rather than a decision

steps.text: Accounts, pipelines, what deploys by hand, what nobody dares touch, and last month's bill.
Every service deployable from a pull request; the infrastructure in code, even if it is ugly code.
Logs, metrics and traces where they are useful; an on-call runbook for each alert that can fire.
Deploy frequency, lead time and the bill, before and after. Your engineers ran the last week.
What broke, what did not, what it cost. Then the next piece, or the handover.

faq.q: AWS, Azure or GCP?
faq.a: Mostly AWS, some Azure. If you are on GCP we will say so on the call rather than learn it on your time.

faq.q: Do we need Kubernetes?
faq.a: Usually not. We have run production on EKS where it earned its keep and on Lambda, Railway and plain containers where it did not. The decision is written down with the reasons.

faq.q: Who is on call?
faq.a: Your team, with our runbook, from week six. Until then we are, and the handover includes a week of us watching them run it.

closing: Show us the deploy you dread. We will make it boring.

name: Legacy modernisation
oneLiner: Rebuilds the in-house team can run
description: Strangler-pattern migrations off the system nobody wants to touch, one bounded piece at a time, with the old and new running side by side until the numbers match.
goodFor: A system nobody wants to touch
A framework three major versions behind
A migration that has been ‘next quarter’ for two years
gets: Strangler-pattern migration: one bounded piece at a time, never a big-bang cutover
Old and new running side by side until the numbers match
Parity measured: same inputs, same outputs, in your environment, before anything is switched off
Knowledge captured where your team looks, not in our heads
sayNoWhen: Rewrite it all is the plan, and the only plan
Nobody can say what the system does today, and nobody wants to find out

steps.text: What the system does, who depends on it, and where it can be cut without anyone noticing.
The smallest valuable piece chosen; a test that replays real inputs through old and new.
New code taking real traffic for one bounded piece; the old path still there, one flag away.
The same loop, piece by piece, each one measured, each one reversible.
What moved, what matched, what the old system still owns. Then the next seam.

faq.q: How long does a migration take?
faq.a: Longer than a rewrite is promised to take and shorter than a rewrite actually takes. The first seam is live in six weeks; after that you can see the rate and decide the pace.

faq.q: What if the old system has no tests?
faq.a: Then the parity test is the first thing we write: real inputs recorded, replayed through both paths, differences listed. It is the only safe way to learn what the system does.

faq.q: Can we stop halfway?
faq.a: Yes, and the system is better than when we started: the pieces already moved keep running, and the map of the rest is yours.

closing: Name the system nobody touches. We will say where to cut first.

name: Mobile
oneLiner: iOS and Android without two teams
description: Cross-platform where it makes sense, native where it does not, with the release pipeline and crash reporting set up before the first store submission.
goodFor: A web product that needs to be in the stores
An app with more crashes than reviews
Two native teams doing the same work twice
gets: One codebase where the product allows; native where it does not, and the decision written down
Store-ready from the start: signing, review guidelines, a release pipeline before the first submission
Crash reporting and analytics from day one, not after the first one-star review
Offline-first where the device will actually be offline
sayNoWhen: The app is a website in a wrapper and should stay a website
Two native teams are wanted for reasons that are not about the product

steps.text: What the app must do on a bad network, what it needs from the device, and who installs it.
Signing, TestFlight and Play tracks, crash reporting, analytics. Before the first screen.
A real journey end to end, on real devices, measured.
Review guidelines handled before review, not after rejection.
Crash-free rate, adoption, the next journey. Your call.

faq.q: Native or cross-platform?
faq.a: Depends on the product, not on us. We have shipped Kotlin, custom Android (AOSP) players, and cross-platform builds; the decision goes in the SOW with the reasons.

faq.q: Do you handle the app stores?
faq.a: Yes: accounts, signing, review guidelines, the release notes. If Apple rejects a build, that is our problem on our time.

faq.q: What about devices that are offline for days?
faq.a: Offline-first sync is something we have built for signage players that lose their connection for a week; the app keeps working and reconciles when it can.

closing: Tell us what the app must do offline. We will say how.

name: QA & test automation
description: Unit, integration and end-to-end coverage that runs in CI in minutes, plus load testing before the launch rather than after the outage.
goodFor: Releases that break something every time
A test suite everyone skips
A launch with no idea what load it takes
gets: Unit, integration and end-to-end coverage that runs in CI in minutes
Flaky tests tracked and fixed, not retried until green
Load testing before the launch, not after the outage
The same discipline for AI features: an evaluation harness that gates release
sayNoWhen: Coverage is wanted as a number rather than as fewer incidents
Tests are wanted so that nobody has to review

steps.text: What exists, what is skipped, what is flaky, and how long a green build takes today.

steps.what: A gate on every pull request
steps.text: The suite runs in CI in minutes; a red build blocks the merge, and everyone can see why.

steps.what: End to end on the journeys that matter
steps.text: The five flows that would make the phone ring, covered on real browsers and devices.
The launch load, run before the launch; your team owns the suite and the flake board.
Build time, flake rate, incidents, before and after. Then the next gap.

faq.q: What tools?
faq.a: Playwright, pytest, Jest and k6 for most stacks, plus generated tests and guardrails from our agentic pipeline where the codebase suits it. The tool follows the stack; we do not make you adopt ours.

faq.q: Will tests slow the team down?
faq.a: A suite that runs in minutes speeds the team up; one that takes an hour gets skipped. The first thing we measure is build time, and it goes down before coverage goes up.

faq.q: Can you test the AI features too?
faq.a: Yes. Evaluation harnesses are tests: a labelled set, a number, a gate in CI. We have shipped them for computer vision, recommendation and retrieval features.

closing: Show us the suite everyone skips. We will make it trusted.
